# Lynn Conway: Key Contributions and Legacy
Lynn Conway was a pioneering computer scientist and electrical engineer whose work profoundly influenced the semiconductor industry. After early research at IBM, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling for the ACS supercomputer project (a precursor to the "superscalar" architecture), she was dismissed from her position in 1968 when she revealed her intention to transition genders. Conway subsequently rebuilt her career, working at Computer Applications, Inc., Memorex, and then at Xerox PARC, where she led the "LSI Systems" group. Her collaboration with Carver Mead led to the co-authorship of "Introduction to VLSI Systems," a foundational textbook that helped usher in the VLSI design revolution, fostered scalable design rules, and facilitated university adoption of chip design education. She played a vital role in developing the MOSIS system—an internet-based rapid prototyping and manufacturing system that made state-of-the-art chip fabrication accessible to universities and startups.
Conway's influence extended beyond technology. As she neared retirement, she began sharing her story as a transgender woman, becoming a prominent activist for transgender rights, equal opportunities, and employment protections—particularly in the high-tech industry. She maintained resources and a website to support trans individuals and advocated for LGBT inclusivity in professional codes of ethics. Conway received numerous honors, including induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, multiple honorary doctorates, and recognition as a "Stonewall 40 trans hero" and one of Time Magazine's "21 Transgender People Who Influenced American Culture." She died in June 2024 at age 86, and her legacy continues as both a technological trailblazer and a role model for inclusively in STEM.
